content: The DEFINE trial was a 76-week, global, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study designed to evaluate the tolerability and efficacy of anacetrapib, a cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitor, when added to ongoing statin therapy in patients with coronary heart disease (CHD) or CHD risk-equivalent conditions. The study was sponsored by Merck and registered under ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT00685776. The primary objective of the trial was to assess the therapeutic and adverse effects of anacetrapib, both alone and in combination with statins. The study included patients with CHD or CHD risk-equivalent conditions who were already on statin therapy with well-controlled low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C). For the extension phase, patients were required to have completed the base study, including a reversibility period of 12 to 24 weeks, and to have continued statin therapy with or without additional lipid-modifying treatments. Patients were excluded from the trial if they had a history of heart failure, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, or stroke within three months prior to screening. Other exclusion criteria included uncontrolled hypertension, uncontrolled hypercholesterolemia, liver disease, mental instability, substance abuse within the past five years, pregnancy or breastfeeding, recent cancer diagnosis, HIV positivity, recent blood donation, or participation in another investigational drug study within the last 30 days. The primary outcome of the study was the reduction in LDL-C levels compared to placebo. Secondary outcomes included an increase in high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C) levels and safety assessments, such as adverse events, vital signs, electrocardiograms (ECGs), physical examinations, and laboratory tests. The results of the trial demonstrated that 17.6% of patients on anacetrapib were discontinued due to LDL-C levels dropping below 25 mg/dL at two consecutive visits, compared to only 0.1% in the placebo group. Anacetrapib significantly reduced LDL-C levels by 39.8% at 24 weeks, with LDL-C decreasing from 81 mg/dL to 45 mg/dL. In contrast, the placebo group only experienced a modest reduction in LDL-C from 82 mg/dL to 77 mg/dL. HDL-C levels increased by 138.1% in the anacetrapib group, rising from 41 mg/dL to 101 mg/dL, compared to a smaller increase in the placebo group from 40 mg/dL to 46 mg/dL. These changes were statistically significant (p<0.001). Patients with baseline low HDL-C levels (<40 mg/dL) experienced an even greater increase in HDL-C, with a 152% rise in this subgroup. Anacetrapib also led to significant reductions in apolipoprotein B (apoB), non-HDL-C, lipoprotein(a), and triglycerides, as well as an increase in apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I) levels. These effects were sustained throughout the 76-week follow-up period. During the reversibility phase, 1,398 patients were enrolled, and the lipid-altering effects of anacetrapib persisted, albeit at reduced levels (50-60% of the on-treatment values). Trace concentrations of anacetrapib were still detectable in patients during this phase. Anacetrapib was not associated with a significant increase in adverse events compared to placebo. However, patients on anacetrapib had a significantly lower incidence of liver function test abnormalities (p=0.02). Additionally, serum sodium levels decreased by 0.96 mmol/L in the anacetrapib group compared to a 1.2 mmol/L decrease in the placebo group (p=0.02). Post-hoc analyses revealed that patients on anacetrapib had significantly fewer revascularization procedures (p=0.001) and cardiovascular events (p=0.048) compared to the placebo group. The percentage of patients who discontinued the study due to two consecutive LDL-C levels below 25 mg/dL was 14.6% in the anacetrapib group and 17.4% in the placebo group. In conclusion, anacetrapib was associated with a significant reduction in LDL-C and a substantial increase in HDL-C, with a favorable safety profile. Further clinical trials are necessary to confirm the potential cardiovascular benefits of increasing HDL-C levels in high-risk patients.
